name: clickhouse-cpp
baseline: ClickHouse HTTP interface via curl; official clickhouse-jdbc (Java, HTTP), ClickHouse/clickhouse-go and Python clickhouse-driver clients
workload: Client overhead reading SELECT number FROM system.numbers_mt LIMIT 500000000 (500 million UInt64 rows, 4.0 GB) from a localhost ClickHouse server, wall time and client RAM per library.
claimed_speedup: clickhouse-cpp 516ms / 6.9M RAM vs curl (C, HTTP) 3.7s, clickhouse-jdbc (Java, HTTP) 7.2s, clickhouse-driver (Python) 37s, ClickHouse/clickhouse-go (Go) 46.8s; the page's own ratio column gives clickhouse-cpp 1.47x, curl 9x, clickhouse-jdbc 18x, clickhouse-driver Python 106x, clickhouse-go 117x relative to the ~1x leaders (about 7.2x vs curl, 14x vs clickhouse-jdbc, 72x vs Python clickhouse-driver, 91x vs clickhouse-go, derived from page data). Not the fastest client: ch-go 401ms and the C++ clickhouse-client 387ms are faster.
tradeoffs: Native binary protocol client with a columnar Block API, so it avoids per-row parsing but the caller works with column blocks; C++17; built with CMake or Bazel.
caveats: Evidence lives in the separate ClickHouse/ch-bench repo (Apache-2.0, 36 stars), whose README calls it 'Totally unscientific and mostly unrealistic' and says the ClickHouse/ch-go project uses it to understand its own performance. It measures one synthetic query on localhost; CPU model, compiler and C++ build flags are not stated (the Makefile builds only the Go and Rust programs; ch-bench-cpp/bench.cpp has no build line) and ClickHouse server version is not stated, so it cannot reach tier A. The README notes row-oriented libraries pay per-row overhead and the reflection-based Go drivers carry extra overhead. The wins are mostly native binary protocol vs HTTP and vs Go/Java/Python clients; against other native C++/Go clients it is slower (1.47x the leader; the README's C++ hyperfine table puts clickhouse-cpp at 574.4 ms vs clickhouse-client 561.9 ms, about parity). The repo's own bench/bench.cpp (Google Benchmark, SelectNumber over 1000 rows) has no baseline.

name: DoltLite
baseline: SQLite (stock SQLite built from the reference amalgamation by test/build_stock_reference.sh)
workload: Sysbench-style SQL workloads (oltp_point_select, range selects, updates, inserts, joins; 100,000-row fixtures, integer, text, blob and composite primary keys), in-memory and file-backed, run through the same C timer harness against both engines on a GitHub-hosted runner, paired alternating runs, medians.
claimed_speedup: No overall speedup claimed; the report is a regression gate with slowdown ceilings. Integer-key file-backed rows where DoltLite is faster (time, SQLite then DoltLite): oltp_point_select 64.75ms vs 30.79ms (0.5x time), select_random_ranges 7.90ms vs 4.29ms (0.5x), oltp_read_only 126.32ms vs 81.03ms (0.6x), file-backed oltp_write_only 80.38ms vs 59.68ms (0.7x). Aggregates are slower: in-memory reads 9.57s vs 11.12s (1.2x), in-memory writes 1.94s vs 3.03s (1.6x), file-backed reads 10.16s vs 11.24s (1.1x), file-backed writes 3.66s vs 4.03s (1.1x), autocommit writes 816.91ms vs 2.35s (2.9x slower).
compiler_and_flags: cc -O2 -Werror for the sysbench_timer.c harness, linked to libdoltlite.a or the stock-reference sqlite3.o (compiler version not stated in the nightly workflow); DoltLite library built with ./configure && make (flags not read).
hardware: GitHub-hosted runner (runs-on ubuntu-latest, image ubuntu24 20260927.320.1); CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Replaces SQLite's B-tree with a content-addressed prolly tree to give Git-like version control (branch, merge, diff, history) on a SQL database; stores in a single-file chunk store, so the file format is not SQLite-compatible. Durable autocommit writes cost about 3x SQLite. Project is labelled Beta.
caveats: Not a speed claim: the project's own docs say the nightly comparison tracks 'the remaining SQL performance gap' and gate DoltLite at up to 2.3x slower per workload (5.5x for autocommit). Rows where DoltLite wins are per-workload file-backed rows from the report's detail tables (cited from the integer-key table); the summed file-backed read total is still 1.1x slower, and in the blob and composite key tables file-backed oltp_write_only is 1.2x and 1.3x slower. Hardware is a shared CI runner with no CPU model, so tier C. A DoltHub blog post ('How fast is DoltLite', 2026-06-08) says reads are about 5% faster to parity on file-backed databases and writes about 40% slower; dolthub.com is blocked here so that comes from a search snippet only. The README describes the project as the product of agentic engineering.
